title: Chardonnay
description: The world's most famous white grape: a neutral canvas for place and winemaking, from Chablis to Champagne.
L: Explain why it's called a canvas

Chardonnay can taste of green apple and lemon, or peach and melon, or pineapple and mango, depending on climate. Winemaking adds butter, toast, vanilla, hazelnut or cream. Acidity ranges from high to medium, body from light to full. With Spain's Airén, it's one of the two most planted white grapes in the world.
Climate sets fruit; winemaking adds the rest

DNA shows Chardonnay is a cross of Pinot Noir and Gouais Blanc, probably in Burgundy in the Middle Ages. It's named after the village of Chardonnay, in the Mâconnais. Its own aromas are fairly neutral, so it reflects site and winemaking clearly. It buds early, risking frost, but ripens reliably.
Why is Chardonnay called a winemaker's canvas?
Its own aromas are neutral, so it reflects site and winemaking
Neutral fruit lets climate and winemaking choices show clearly.

Because it varies so much, look for clues: high acidity and green fruit with a chalky edge suggest cool Chablis; nutty, buttery richness with toast suggests oaked Burgundy or California; tropical fruit and soft acidity suggest a warm climate. A lack of strong aromatic signature is itself a clue.
Chardonnay is a cross of Pinot Noir and Gouais Blanc.
Yes. It's a sibling of Gamay, Aligoté and Melon.
Chardonnay's fruit ranges from apple to pineapple with climate
It's a cross of Pinot Noir and Gouais Blanc from Burgundy
Its neutral character reflects site and winemaking
Explain the ABC backlash and revival

Chardonnay's home is Burgundy and Champagne. It grows in almost every wine country: California, Australia, Chile, South Africa, New Zealand, Italy, Oregon, Argentina and England. It adapts to cool and warm climates and many soils, though limestone and chalk are prized.

Cool climates, like Chablis, Tasmania or Sonoma Coast, give lean, citrus Chardonnay with high acidity. Moderate climates, like the Côte de Beaune or Margaret River, give stone fruit and balance. Warm climates, like inland California or Australia's Riverland, give tropical fruit and lower acidity.
Match each climate to its Chardonnay.
Climate is the first key to Chardonnay's style.

In the 1990s, heavily oaked, buttery Chardonnays became so common that some drinkers turned away, a trend called ABC, Anything But Chardonnay. Since the 2000s, producers have picked earlier, used less new oak and blocked malolactic more often, giving fresher, more elegant wines.
What did ABC stand for in the 1990s?
A backlash against heavily oaked Chardonnay.
Chardonnay grows almost everywhere, from Burgundy to Chile
Climate shifts it from citrus to tropical
After the ABC backlash, many styles became leaner
Chablis and the Côte de Beaune

Chablis, in northern Burgundy, is cool and continental, with frost risk. Its Kimmeridgian soil, limestone and clay full of tiny oyster fossils, gives lean, mineral, high-acid wines with green apple, lemon and a flinty, saline edge. Most Chablis is unoaked; Grand Crus often see some oak. Levels: Petit Chablis, Chablis, Premier Cru and seven Grand Crus.

In the Côte de Beaune, south of Beaune, Chardonnay makes some of the world's greatest whites. Meursault is rich, nutty and buttery; Puligny-Montrachet elegant and floral; Chassagne-Montrachet fuller. Grand Crus like Le Montrachet and Corton-Charlemagne are fermented and aged in oak, with great ageing potential.
What is special about Chablis' Kimmeridgian soil?
Kimmeridgian limestone and clay are full of fossilised oyster shells.

Chablis is cooler, leaner and more mineral, usually less oak. The Côte de Beaune is warmer, with riper fruit, more body and oak. Further south, the Mâconnais, with Pouilly-Fuissé, gives rounder, fruitier, good-value wines. All are 100% Chardonnay.
Chablis lean; Côte de Beaune rich
Match each wine to its style.
Burgundy shows every side of Chardonnay.
Chablis is lean and mineral on Kimmeridgian soil
The Côte de Beaune makes rich, oaked whites
The Mâconnais gives rounder, good-value wines

Barrel fermentation and ageing add vanilla, toast, spice and a rounder texture. New oak adds more; older barrels mostly add texture and slow oxygen. Burgundy often uses 20 to 50% new oak for top wines. Oak needs ripe, concentrated fruit, or it overwhelms the wine.

Malolactic conversion turns sharp malic acid into softer lactic acid, adding a buttery note from diacetyl and lowering acidity. Lees ageing leaves the wine on dead yeast for months, adding creaminess and protecting it from oxidation. Bâtonnage, stirring the lees, increases these effects. Most Burgundy whites use all three.
Butter from malolactic; cream from lees
Match each technique to its effect.
Each winemaking choice leaves its mark.
If a Chardonnay tastes of butter and popcorn, it went through malolactic. If it tastes of toast and vanilla, it saw new oak. If it's pure lemon and apple, it was probably made in steel.
Which techniques make Chardonnay richer and rounder?
Early picking and steel keep it lean and fresh.
Oak adds vanilla, toast and texture
Malolactic adds butter and softens acidity
Name other sparkling regions using it

Chardonnay is about 30% of Champagne's vineyards, concentrated in the Côte des Blancs, on chalk. It brings finesse, acidity, citrus and floral notes, and the ability to age long. Grand Cru villages like Cramant, Avize, Le Mesnil-sur-Oger and Oger give some of its finest sparkling wines.

Blanc de Blancs, white from whites, is Champagne made only from white grapes, almost always Chardonnay. It's lean and citrus when young, developing brioche, hazelnut and toast with age. Salon, which makes only vintage Blanc de Blancs from Le Mesnil, and Krug's Clos du Mesnil are famous examples.
Blanc de Blancs: white from whites
What is Blanc de Blancs Champagne made from?
Blanc de Blancs means white from whites.

Chardonnay is key in traditional method wines worldwide: Franciacorta, Trentodoc, Crémant de Bourgogne, English sparkling wine, Tasmania and California. Its high acidity in cool climates and neutral fruit take on the bready, toasty notes of lees ageing well.
Which are known for Chardonnay-based sparkling wine?
The Mosel is known for still Riesling.
Chardonnay is about 30% of Champagne, mostly in the Côte des Blancs
Blanc de Blancs is made only from white grapes
Franciacorta, England and Tasmania also use it
Pair different Chardonnay styles with food

Lean Chablis suits oysters, shellfish and goat's cheese. Rich, oaked Chardonnay suits lobster, roast chicken, creamy sauces and pork. Tropical, warm-climate Chardonnay suits grilled chicken and mildly spiced dishes. Blanc de Blancs suits sushi, caviar and fried food.
Chablis with oysters; oaked with lobster

Serve lean Chardonnay at 8 to 10 degrees, rich oaked styles at 10 to 13. Most New World Chardonnay is best within three to five years. Grand Cru Chablis and Côte de Beaune age 10 to 20 years, developing honey, nuts and mushroom. Premature oxidation, or premox, affected some Burgundy from the 1990s.
Which Chardonnay style suits oysters best?
Chablis' acidity and saline edge match oysters.
Serve rich, oaked Chardonnay slightly warmer than other whites. Too cold, its texture and aromas close up.
Some Burgundy whites from the 1990s suffered from premature oxidation.
Yes. Premox affected some vintages, with wines browning and losing fruit early.
Match the Chardonnay style to the dish
Serve lean styles colder, rich ones a little warmer
Match each wine to its style.
What does malolactic conversion add to Chardonnay?
Lactic acid and diacetyl give butter and softness.
Most Chablis is aged in new oak.
Not true. Most Chablis is unoaked; some Grand Crus use oak.
Chardonnay is a cross of Pinot Noir and Gouais Blanc.
Kimmeridgian limestone and clay with oyster fossils.
Chardonnay is neutral, reflecting climate and winemaking
Chablis, the Côte de Beaune and Champagne are its benchmarks
Oak, malolactic and lees shape its richness
It suits everything from oysters to lobster
